Build Your Badge 
 Security BSides Orlando 2026 
 Build Your Badge 
 Your badge arrives part-built. Seven pieces are yours to solder — here's how to do it on your own, at your own pace, without queuing at the Soldering Village. 
 What's in your kit 
 Everything else — the microcontroller, the reverse-mounted LEDs, all the tiny parts — is already soldered on when you pick the badge up. 
 4× LED goes on the front 
 1× SAO connector goes on the front 
 1× Power switch goes on the back 
 1× Battery holder goes on the back 
 1× AAA battery no soldering 
 A suggested order 
 Not a rule, just the order that keeps the board flattest and easiest to hold while you work — lowest parts first, tallest last. 
 Power switch — back 
 The only surface-mount piece, and the fiddliest. Do it while the board is still completely flat. Tack one corner pad, check the switch sits square against the printing, then solder the rest. 
 The four LEDs — front 
 Push them in from the front so the bodies stick out the art side, then turn the badge over and solder the legs on the back. Trim the legs afterwards. 
 SAO connector — front 
 Also fits from the front and solders from behind, so add-ons plug into the art side. 
 Battery holder — back 
 Tallest part, so it goes last. Sits on the back, soldered from the front. 
 Battery in, switch to ON 
 Drop the AAA into the holder and slide the switch to ON . 
 Three things worth slowing down for 
 The SAO notch faces up 
 The six-pin socket only works one way round — notch toward the top edge of the badge. Fitted backwards, anything you plug into it gets power and ground swapped. It's printed on the back of the board if you want to double-check. 
 Square pad takes the short leg

=== profile readme ===
# Hacker Con Badges

**The hardware, firmware and stories behind hacker conference badges worldwide.**

[Explore the catalogue](https://badge.gallery/badges) · [Browse by country](https://badge.gallery/countries) · [Follow the timeline](https://badge.gallery/timeline) · [How we document](https://badge.gallery/methodology) · [Repository inventory](https://github.com/badge-gallery/.github/tree/main/preservation)

Hacker badges carry a piece of their event with them: a radio experiment, a tiny synthesizer, a puzzle, a game, or a platform people keep building on long after the conference ends.

[badge.gallery](https://badge.gallery) documents those artifacts and the people who made them. The catalogue connects hardware specifications, firmware, app stores, add-ons, repair notes, event history and original sources. It also records non-electronic identity artifacts when that is what the evidence supports.

## Keeping badges usable

This organization is the home for our developing firmware preservation and restoration effort. Native GitHub forks and explicitly licensed source mirrors have been preserved under readable project and component names; browse the [repository inventory](https://github.com/badge-gallery/.github/tree/main/preservation) for their upstream source mapping and collection status. Builds and hardware restorations have not yet been tested. Broader artifact preservation work will be added in the future.

Our approach:

- **Preserve the originals.** Retain upstream history, releases, provenance and author credits.
- **Make builds repeatable.** Record toolchains, dependencies, source revisions and build results.
- **Document what works.** Keep successful builds and tests on physical hardware distinct, including board revisions and known limitations.

 🔍 "> Build Your Badge Security BSides Orlando 2026 Build Your Badge Your badge arrives part-built. Seven pieces are yours to solder — here's how to do it on your own, at your own pace, without queuing at the Soldering Village. What's in your kit Everything else — the microcontroller, the reverse-mounted LEDs, all the tiny parts — is already soldered on when you pick the badge up. 4× LED goes on the front 1× SAO connector goes on the front 1× Power switch goes on the back 1× Battery holder goes on the back 1× AAA battery no soldering A suggested order Not a rule, just the order that keeps the board flattest and easiest to hold while you work — lowest parts first, tallest last. Power switch — back The only surface-mount piece, and the fiddliest. Do it while the board is still completely flat. Tack one corner pad, check the switch sits square against the printing, then solder the rest. The four LEDs — front Push them in from the front so the bodies stick out the art side, then turn the badge over and solder the legs on the back. Trim the legs afterwards. SAO connector — front Also fits from the front and solders from behind, so add-ons plug into the art side. Battery holder — back Tallest part, so it goes last. Sits on the back, soldered from the front. Battery in, switch to ON Drop the AAA into the holder and slide the switch to ON . Three things worth slowing down for The SAO notch faces up The six-pin socket only works one way round — notch toward the top edge of the badge. Fitted backwards, anything you plug into it gets power and ground swapped. It's printed on the back of the board if you want to double-check. Square pad takes the short leg Each LED has one square pad and one round one. The square pad takes the shorter leg — the one on the flat side of the LED body. Backwards, the LED simply never lights. No harm done, but you'll be desoldering it to turn it round. The switch will test your patience Six small pads and nothing holding

The rev R1 schematic instantiates a CH32V003F4P6 RISC-V microcontroller, three SK6812MINI-E reverse-mount addressable LEDs, the retained Breathing and Fast Blink 3 mm LEDs, an SAO v2 expansion socket with ESD protection, a single AAA cell with a TPS61021A boost converter, and the MST22D18G2 power switch, and the repository carried generated JLCPCB Gerbers, BOM, and CPL files. The official event site sets the conference for September 26 at Full Sail Live in Winter Park, Florida. At the September 25 recheck, one day before the conference, the entire 2026-badge repository, its file tree, and its commit history were no longer publicly reachable while the organization and its prior-year repositories remained public and the site still named no badge.
